A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [a,b]$ has the position vector

$$

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
r(x,\theta )=⟨x,\,\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,x\in [-1,1],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

questions.problem:
$$
⟨\text{_______}\,,\,-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y={x}^{2}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [0,1]$ is given above. What is the $1$st component of the product?
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $y={x}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)={x}^{2},$ and 

$$
D=\{(x,\theta )\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$

$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}

Since $f=\sqrt{z-1},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z-1}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is 

$$

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=e^{x/2}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis for $x \in [0,2]$ is given by

$$
\big\langle \text{_______}\,, \:-e^{x/2} \cos\theta, \: -e^{x/2}\sin\theta \big\rangle.
$$

What is the $1$st component of the product?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $y=e^{x/2} \geq 0$ for all $x \in [0,2].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)=e^{x/2},$ and 

$$
D = \big\{ (x,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi \big\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=e^{x/2},$ we obtain $f' = \dfrac12 e^{x/2}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x},\,-{e}^{x/2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{e}^{x/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $1$st component of the product is $\dfrac{1}{2}e^x.$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(z)=\sin z,$ we obtain $f'(z) = \cos z.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡z\sqrt{1+(\operatorname{cos}⁡z)^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡z\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡z}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Consider the planar curve $y=e^{-x}$ defined on the interval $x \in [0,2],$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14275690/assets/a8ce2449af085548fecc543fbd5ccfec0e8024344547b2a7825f3a6e9ccf63d4.png)

 

By rotating this curve $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a **surface of revolution**:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14275690/assets/88c9c1ec629ab9967cc011aaadafebea255cd50abee9c3730bed4f53f671c71b.png)

 

We can parametrize this surface in the following way:

- We take a point $P$ on the surface with $x$-coordinate equal to $x_0$ for some fixed $x_0 \in [0,2].$

- Now, by taking the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=x_0,$ we get a circle of radius $e^{-x_0}.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14275690/assets/f1e2cf1c571a21e06f1b25f99a64b5529fea8c65c897b3f225cfd0d307d725d7.png)

 
This circle can be parameterized as follows:

$$
\mathbf r(x_0, \theta) = \big\langle {\color{black}x_0}, \: e^{-x_0} \, \cos{\theta}, \: e^{-x_0} \, \sin{\theta} \big\rangle,
\quad  \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

- Finally, by allowing $x_0$ to vary over the interval $[0, 2],$ these circles will trace out the surface of revolution. Therefore, our parameterization is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = \big\langle x, \: e^{-x} \cos{\theta}, \: e^{-x}\sin{\theta} \big\rangle,
\quad 
x \in [0,2], 
\quad
\theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

Let's now describe some general formulas for parametrizing surfaces of revolution.

tutorials.name: Parametrizing a Surface Generated by Rotating y=y(x) About the x-Axis
tutorials.problem:
Consider the point $(x,y(x),0)$ that lies on the curve $y=y(x)$ in the $xy$-plane. Rotating this point by $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis generates a circle, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14275690/assets/86cbc06bd3730430665744216a702ed29cc75acae33a569e00636ee53149065d.png)

In the diagram above, the pair $(\textrm{circle}_1,\textrm{circle}_2)$ denotes any parametrization of a circle of radius $y(x)$ with parameter $x.$

In general, given a curve $y=y(x)\geq 0$ for $x \in [a,b]$ that is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, the corresponding surface of revolution can be parametrized as

$$
\mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: y(x) \cos\theta, \: y(x) \sin\theta \big\rangle, \quad x\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi).
$$

Since a parametrization of a circle is not unique, we can obtain different parameterizations of our surface of revolution. For example, the following is also a valid parameterization:

$$
\mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: y(x) \sin\theta, \: y(x) \cos\theta \big\rangle, \quad x\in[a,b], \quad \theta\in [0,2\pi)
$$

tutorials.name: Computing a Surface Area of Revolution
tutorials.problem:
Recall that if $S$ is a surface parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

defined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \: \textrm{d}S =  \iint\limits_{D} \| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| \: \textrm{d}A,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.

Let's apply this formula to find the surface area generated by a surface of revolution.
